turn_text: Hi there and welcome to the Manufacturing Report for the week of April 10. I'm Scott Paul, President of the Alliance for American Manufacturing and host of this podcast. You can find this and past episodes of the Manufacturing Report on iTunes and SoundCloud and on our Facebook page at American Manufacturing. If you'd like to hear more of this, please take a moment to like the podcast and perhaps even write a review and share with a friend who would enjoy hearing the Manufacturing Report. You can tweet us at KeepIt Made in USA and you can connect with us on our website, americanmanufacturing.org. This week we'll explore buying American with your tax dollars and how this issue could create an unlikely alliance between Senate Democrats and President Trump if the White House follows through on its plan. Let's get started. President Donald Trump has been proclaiming his bi-American, higher American plan frequently. But what does the president mean when he says this? America has had bi-America policies on the books for more than 80 years. It means that certain types of goods made possible by federal spending, like assembling warplanes or building bridges, must be made in America. We at the Alliance for American Manufacturing have been working on this issue for the past decade. And for the better part of that, so has Wisconsin Senator Tammy Baldwin. Senator Baldwin has been a great leader on by America policies and in particular on ensuring our nation's water infrastructure. Everything from manhole covers on sewers to the water pipes that bring drinking water to our homes are made in America. I had a chance to sit down with Senator Baldwin, who has written a new piece of legislation to strengthen by America laws to get her take on working with the president on by America policies, as well as where she sees America's trade agenda heading. Let's have a listen. And I'm honored to have as a guest Senator Tammy Baldwin from the great state of Wisconsin. Thank you for joining us on the Manufacturing Report, Senator Baldwin.

turn_text: And thank you as well for all of your leadership on by America policies. I know this is important to manufacturers and workers in Wisconsin and they very much appreciate your leadership on this. You recently brought to light some findings of a GAO report that established that the United States isn't winning in the procurement game when it comes to serving our own market.

Absolutely. This was an interest of mine for some years, and I joined up with colleague Senator Merkley to request an in-depth study of how some of our bilateral and multilateral trade deals impact by America provisions, procurement preferences, if you will. And what we discovered is by including them in trade deals, we really provide way too much wiggle room that basically allows multinational manufacturers to compete for government opportunities as though they were domestic corporations and foreign companies to do the same. And that's distressing because I want to be able to tell taxpayers in my state that when their hard-earned tax dollars are being spent on various government activities, including infrastructure, that it is supporting American products and American jobs.

turn_text: Well, it seems to me that if the White House wanted to reach out and build those bridges to a lot of the industrial state Democrats, like you who have been working on trade reform and procurement issues, for years that there's a majority position to be had there, but it's kind of getting them to translate rhetoric into policy. Yeah, so I've been seeing probably what everybody else has been looking at, a sort of draft that was leaked out of the White House about how they might proceed with changing and renegotiating aspects of NAFTA. And so I was looking for and hoping for sort of more robust interest in changing language, renegotiating language. And particularly along the lines that we've been talking about, whether it's procurement or things like how disputes are settled. And I didn't see enough change.
